cards.name: Clean natural correction
cards.summary: A neutral, honest fix for a flat or slightly dark photo: shadows opened, a little contrast and colour, nothing that reads as a filter.
use_for: news, documentary and event photos that must stay truthful
product and catalogue photos before layout
a first pass before any creative grade
batch-correcting a shoot to one baseline
avoid: adding, removing or moving content in a news or documentary photo: keep every change global and tonal
a photo that is already well exposed: Shadows/Highlights then only flattens it; skip that step
strong colour casts: neutralise with Temperature / Tint first and check skin and greys
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object on the photo layer, so the filter that follows stays an editable smart filter.

Image > Adjustments > Shadows/Highlights on the smart object: the default Shadows amount (35 %) opens the darks; Color Correction 20 keeps the lifted shadows from going grey. The Shadows / Highlights amounts travel in object params a plan cannot carry; set them in the scripting call (the card's example uses 50 / 15) if the default is too strong.
Brightness/Contrast adjustment layer above: Contrast (key center) +12 restores the punch Shadows/Highlights takes away; the non-legacy mode protects the ends.

Color and vibrance adjustment layer on top: Vibrance +15 lifts muted colours and spares skin; Temperature / Tint stay 0 unless a cast needs neutralising (the render showed Temperature -50 is a strong cool shift, so move it in single digits).
Effects > Adjust > Auto Adjust on the bitmap: stretches each channel to the full range, a mild contrast and cast fix on a flat photo.
Effects > Adjust > Gamma: in CorelDRAW values above 1 lighten the midtones; 1.1 opens the shadows a touch while black and white hold.
Effects > Adjust > Vibrance: +15 for richer muted colours without clipping the vivid ones.

cards.name: Cinematic teal and orange
cards.summary: The blockbuster grade: shadows pushed toward teal, highlights and warm tones toward orange, with a little extra contrast.
use_for: film-poster and trailer-style key art
travel and lifestyle social posts
YouTube thumbnails and banners that want a movie feel
unifying photos from different cameras into one look
avoid: skin-heavy close-ups: too much orange turns skin brown; keep the gradient layer at 30-40 % opacity
news photos: a stylised grade changes how the scene reads
CorelDRAW: no scripted split toning on a colour photo (its Color Balance render failed and Tone Curve needs input); grade in Photoshop
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Gradient Map adjustment layer: stops dark teal #12333A (location 0) to warm orange #F0A060 (location 4096), sent in the With (gradient) object exactly as in the card's scripting (the stop() helper). The render test used the default black-to-white gradient (pass); a coloured gradient is not render-tested, so this recipe stays at medium.

Set the gradient map layer to Soft Light (layer.blendMode = BlendMode.SOFTLIGHT) at 40-60 % layer opacity (layer.opacity): the map now tints shadows teal and lights orange instead of replacing the colours. Its card verdict 'wrong' was about the plate sentence; the frame matched the Soft Light formula.
Color and vibrance layer: Vibrance +20 brings back colour richness, Saturation -5 keeps the oranges from clipping.
Brightness/Contrast layer: Contrast +15 for the cinematic punch.

manual_steps: Judge the teal / orange balance on screen: the stop colours and the layer opacity are taste, and the coloured gradient map has no render test yet.

cards.name: Warm nostalgic
cards.summary: A soft, warm, slightly faded memory look: amber cast, gentler colour, a light vignette and fine grain.
use_for: throwback and anniversary posts
family, food and travel photos with a cosy mood
festival greetings and invitation backgrounds
lifestyle brand imagery with a vintage feel
avoid: already warm indoor photos: they go muddy orange; lower the filter density or skip it
product shots where colour accuracy matters
heavy grain on images that will be shrunk for social: it turns to mush; keep Amount low
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object on the photo layer, so the filter that follows stays an editable smart filter.
Filter > Lens Correction on the smart object, used only for its vignette: -35 darkens the corners gently (the render at -100 was a heavy vignette); geometry correction off so nothing else moves.
Photo Filter adjustment layer, orange #EC8A00: the render at density 80 gave a strong warm cast, 25-35 is a gentle amber.
Color and vibrance layer: Vibrance -15 / Saturation -5 mute the colours for the faded feel; Temperature +10 adds warmth (negative values cool, as the render showed).
Brightness/Contrast layer: a little lighter and softer (Contrast -10).
Grain adjustment layer on top: fine film grain (Amount 25); the render at Amount 80 was clearly visible even at 960 px.

Effects > Adjust > White Balance on the bitmap: values below the 5000 K default warm the image (the 8500 K render turned it cool); 4000 K is a soft amber shift. The warm direction itself was not rendered.
Effects > Adjust > Vibrance: negative values mute the colours for the faded feel.
Effects > Creative > Vignette: a low Offset keeps the dark border thin (the Offset 50 render left only a small central ellipse), Fade 70 for a soft edge.
Effects > Noise > Add Noise: light Gaussian grain in brightness only (ColorMode Intensity), not the coloured specks of ColorMode Random.

cards.note: CorelDRAW's warm White Balance direction is read from the card's measured cool render, not from a warm render, so the recipe stays at medium; the Photoshop plan is render-verified step by step.

cards.name: Faded matte film
cards.summary: Lifted, matte blacks, lower contrast and softened colour with grain: the faded film-stock look of lifestyle and editorial feeds.
use_for: lifestyle, fashion and café photography
moody social feeds and story backgrounds
quote cards and text-over-photo layouts (lifted blacks keep type readable)
softening harsh phone photos
avoid: prints on uncoated paper: lifted blacks look washed out; lift less
low-light photos with noise: the lifted shadows reveal it; denoise first
the classic route is a Curves layer with the black point raised, but Curves rendered as a no-op in the harness (untested), so this recipe uses a fill layer in Lighten instead
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > New Fill Layer > Solid Color at the top of the stack, colour #262626 (dark grey, sent in the contentLayer descriptor's color).

Set the fill layer to Lighten: every pixel darker than the fill lifts to it (max(base, layer), the formula the render matched; the 'wrong' verdict was the plate sentence), giving flat matte blacks. A lighter grey fades more.
Color and vibrance layer: Vibrance -20 / Saturation -10 soften the colour; Temperature +5 keeps it from going cold.
Brightness/Contrast layer: Contrast -12 for the low-contrast film feel.
Grain layer on top: visible but fine grain.
Effects > Adjust > Gamma 1.25: lifts the darks most (the 2.5 render raised near-black 8 to 63) while white holds, a faded tone curve.
Effects > Adjust > Vibrance: mutes the colours.
Effects > Noise > Add Noise: brightness-only film grain.

manual_steps: CorelDRAW: for truly flat blacks lay a dark-grey rectangle over the photo and set its transparency merge mode to If Lighter on the Transparency tool's property bar (PGD has no scripted card for that merge mode).
cards.note: Photoshop plan: every visual step is render-verified; CorelDRAW only approximates matte blacks with a gamma lift.

cards.name: High-contrast black and white
cards.summary: A punchy monochrome with deep blacks, bright whites and crisp midtone detail, colour channels mixed for drama.
use_for: documentary and street-photo treatments
poster and editorial portraits
making mixed-colour photos sit together in a layout
a base for duotone or spot-colour printing
avoid: a flat grey result from plain desaturation: use the channel mix, not Desaturate
skies and smooth skin at high Clarity: they get gritty; keep Clarity under 30
Illustrator: Convert to Grayscale there changes vector fill and stroke colours, not placed photos; convert the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW

steps.note: Black & White adjustment layer: lighter reds and yellows, darker blues for a dramatic sky; the key 'grain' is the green slider (it reads back under that name).
Brightness/Contrast layer: Contrast +40 for deep blacks and bright whites (non-legacy keeps the ends from clipping hard).
Clarity and dehaze layer: midtone crispness; the render at 60 / 50 was strongly darker and crisper, so keep it moderate.
Effects > Adjust > Black & White with the same channel weights (range -200 to 300).
Effects > Adjust > Auto Adjust: stretches the tones to full black and white.
Effects > Adjust > Gamma 0.85: darkens the midtones for extra drama (values below 1 darken).

cards.name: Two-colour duotone poster
cards.summary: The photo rebuilt in two brand colours, dark colour in the shadows and light colour in the highlights, for bold posters and covers.
use_for: event and music posters
brand hero images in two brand colours
social carousels with a consistent colour identity
covers where a busy photo must sit behind type
avoid: two colours of similar lightness: the image loses all depth; pick one dark and one light colour
real two-ink print jobs: build a true Duotone (Photoshop Image > Mode > Duotone, CorelDRAW Bitmaps > Mode > Duotone) with the printer's inks
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Black & White layer first: controls which colours land in the dark or light ink (these are the defaults; shift them per photo).
Brightness/Contrast layer: Contrast +20 so the two colours separate cleanly.

Gradient Map layer on top: stops dark navy #1D1E4E (location 0) to coral #FF5A5F (location 4096) in the With (gradient) object, as in the card's scripting. The render test used the default black-to-white gradient (pass); a coloured gradient is not render-tested, so this recipe stays at medium.
Effects > Adjust > Black & White on the bitmap (optional; the lens works on colour too).

A rectangle the size of the photo, on top, with a Custom Color Map lens (Shape.CreateLens type 10): Color1 takes the shadows and Color2 the lights, as the render showed (violet darks, amber lights). Direct blend (0) keeps the route between the two colours straight.

manual_steps: For a print duotone with real inks: Photoshop Image > Mode > Grayscale, then Image > Mode > Duotone (no confirmed script route; set inks and curves in the dialog), or CorelDRAW Bitmaps > Mode > Duotone (8-bit).
cards.note: CorelDRAW plan is render-verified (Custom Color Map lens pass); the Photoshop coloured gradient map is not.

cards.name: Cross-processed colour
cards.summary: The look of slide film developed in the wrong chemistry: blue-shifted shadows, yellow-green highlights, high saturation and contrast.
use_for: fashion and music editorial
retro 90s and lo-fi social posts
bold nightlife and festival flyers
avoid: skin-critical portraits: the green highlights make skin sickly; mask the face area out of the gradient layer
corporate or news imagery
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Gradient Map layer: stops deep blue #1B2470 (location 0) to pale yellow-green #E6F07A (location 4096) in the With (gradient) object. The render test used the default black-to-white gradient (pass); a coloured gradient is not render-tested, so this recipe stays at medium.
Gradient map layer to Soft Light at about 50 % opacity: blue shadows, yellow-green lights over the original colour.
Color and vibrance layer: Vibrance +30 / Saturation +10 for the saturated cross-process colour; Tint -10 leans green (Camera Raw sign convention; the tint direction was not separated in the render).
Brightness/Contrast layer: Contrast +30.

manual_steps: CorelDRAW: Effects > Camera > Time Machine has a Cross Process style, but the process could not be chosen by script (the render used the dialog's stored process): pick Cross Process in the dialog by hand, Intensity 60-80, Photo edges off.

cards.name: Single-colour accent pop
cards.summary: Everything goes black and white except one colour family (a brand colour, a product, a warm orange garment), which keeps its colour and pops.
use_for: highlighting a product or brand colour in a photo
social posts where one element must lead the eye
editorial covers with a single colour accent
advertising visuals built around one signature colour
avoid: photos where the accent colour also appears in the background: it stays coloured there too; paint the mask by hand
colour families that blend into skin (reds, oranges): skin may keep colour; tighten the fuzziness or mask by hand
CorelDRAW: PGD has no scripted per-hue selection there (Replace Colors and Selective Color need input); do it in Photoshop
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Select > Color Range: Colors = the family closest to the accent (Reds, Yellows, Greens, Cyans, Blues, Magentas) or sampled colours, Fuzziness about 40 (verified live with Reds / 40).
Select > Inverse: now everything except the accent is selected.
Select > Modify > Feather 1-2 px so the colour edge is not jagged.

Black & White adjustment layer made while the selection is active: Photoshop turns the selection into the layer's mask, so only the non-accent areas lose colour (standard behaviour; the masked result itself is not render-tested).

manual_steps: Check the mask at 100 %: paint white on the Black & White layer's mask where stray accent-coloured areas kept their colour, black where the accent lost it.

cards.name: Brand-colour monotone wash
cards.summary: The whole photo toned in one brand colour (any hue: a warm orange, a corporate blue), lightness kept, for consistent branded imagery.
use_for: brand-consistent photo backgrounds for posts and banners
covers and section dividers in reports
photos behind type that must not compete with it
unifying stock photos from different sources
avoid: very light brand colours (pastel yellow): the tone shows only in the shadows; use a darker shade of the brand colour
photos where the subject must keep natural colour: use the accent pop recipe instead
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Black & White adjustment layer: a clean monochrome base.
Layer > New Fill Layer > Solid Color on top, in the brand colour (e.g. #E8731C warm orange or #1F4E9C blue).
Set the fill layer to Color (SetLum(layer, Lum(base)), the formula the render matched) at 60-90 % opacity: hue and saturation from the brand colour, lightness from the photo.
Effects > Camera > Colorize on the bitmap: Hue = the brand colour's hue in degrees (25 is a warm orange, about 215 a corporate blue; the render at 200 / 70 gave an all-blue tint), lightness kept.

manual_steps: CorelDRAW non-destructive alternative: a rectangle over the photo with a Tinted Grayscale lens in the brand colour (render-verified with #0038B8).

cards.name: Night-time cool grade
cards.summary: A darker, blue, slightly desaturated grade that reads as dusk or night, for moody or cinematic scenes.
use_for: moody cinematic posters
turning a dull daylight shot into a dusk scene
tech, security or mystery themed visuals
backgrounds for neon or glowing type
avoid: bright midday photos with hard shadows: they look like underexposed day, not night; add a vignette and keep lights glowing
photos with skin in the foreground: cool grades turn skin grey; mask it
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Exposure adjustment layer: about one stop darker (the render showed +1.5 is a strong change), gamma 0.9 deepens the mids.
Color and vibrance layer: Temperature -35 cools strongly (the render at -50 gave a strong blue cast), Vibrance -10 for a muted night palette.
Photo Filter, blue #006DFF at density 20 (the render at 60 was a strong cool lavender cast): a little extra blue in the highlights.
Brightness/Contrast layer: Contrast +10 so the darks do not go muddy.
Effects > Adjust > White Balance: higher Kelvin cools (the 8500 K render gave a strong blue-cyan cast).
Effects > Adjust > Gamma 0.75: darker midtones, black and white held.
Effects > Adjust > Vibrance: muted night colour.

cards.name: Bleach bypass
cards.summary: Silver-retention film look: harsh contrast, crushed and gritty midtones, colour drained to about half, for gritty war, sport or thriller visuals.
use_for: gritty sport, action and thriller posters
industrial and urban photography
dramatic advertising key art
avoid: soft beauty, food and product photography: it makes everything harsh
already high-contrast photos: shadows block up; lower the overlay opacity
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Black & White adjustment layer above the photo.
Set the Black & White layer to Overlay at 50-70 % opacity: its grey version multiplies and screens the photo, adding contrast while draining colour (Overlay formula matched in the render).
Color and vibrance layer: Saturation -15 drains more colour.
Brightness/Contrast layer: Contrast +10 to taste.
Effects > Adjust > Vibrance: drains the colour by about half.
Effects > Adjust > Auto Adjust: full black-to-white range.
Effects > Adjust > Gamma 0.85: heavier midtones.

cards.note: Photoshop plan is the real overlay technique (render-verified parts); the CorelDRAW plan approximates it with desaturation and a gamma curve.

cards.name: Sepia vintage print
cards.summary: A warm brown-toned monochrome with softened contrast, vignette and grain, like an old photographic print.
use_for: heritage, history and anniversary visuals
archival-style photo pages
invitations and certificates with an old-photo feel
avoid: presenting a new photo as a historical document
low-resolution photos: grain and vignette exaggerate the softness
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object on the photo layer, so the filter that follows stays an editable smart filter.
Filter > Lens Correction vignette on the smart object (render at -100 = heavy dark corners).
Hue/Saturation adjustment layer with Colorize on: at its default hue it gives the red-brown monotone the render showed; other hues travel in the Adjustment list (not settable from a plan).
Photo Filter, orange at density 20: shifts the red-brown toward a yellower sepia.
Brightness/Contrast layer: Contrast -10 for the soft old-print tone.
Grain layer on top.
Effects > Camera > Sepia Toning: Amount to age 60 (the render at 100 was a full brown monotone).
Effects > Creative > Vignette, soft dark ellipse.
Effects > Noise > Add Noise: brightness-only grain.

manual_steps: CorelDRAW alternative: Effects > Camera > Time Machine with Photo edges on adds an aged, deckle-edged print border (render-verified); choose the process in the dialog.
